body:
Remote control and autonomous functions

A UAV may be guided directly by a remote pilot, follow a pre-programmed route or use automated functions to assist flight. These methods differ in how flight decisions are made.

Operating methodWhat happensHuman involvement
Direct remote pilotingThe pilot sends commands from a separate location.Continuous control is central.
Automated flight assistanceThe system maintains selected flight conditions.The operator supervises the aircraft.
Pre-programmed flightThe aircraft follows an approved route or task sequence.The operator plans and monitors the mission.
Higher autonomyThe system performs some decisions using sensor inputs and programmed rules.Human oversight depends on the system and applicable rules.

An autopilot can maintain or adjust flight conditions without continuous manual inputs. That does not make every autopilot-equipped aircraft fully autonomous. Likewise, a remotely piloted drone can use automatic stabilisation while the pilot remains responsible for its operation.

Essential elements of a UAS

The flying platform normally carries propulsion equipment, a power source, flight-control equipment and a mission payload. A payload may be a camera, mapping instrument, communication equipment or another item carried to perform the task. The ground control station provides an interface for the operator.

A data link carries information between the aircraft and its control equipment. Depending on the system, this may include control commands, aircraft status, images or other sensor readings. A navigation receiver may use satellite navigation signals, but navigation and communication are different functions: knowing an aircraft's position is not the same as maintaining a control link.

Visual line of sight (VLOS) means operating while the remote pilot or observer can maintain direct visual observation as required by the applicable rules. Beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) means operating beyond that direct visual range. BVLOS does not mean autonomous flight; a distant aircraft may still be remotely controlled or monitored.

What is a counter-UAS system?

A counter-unmanned aircraft system (C-UAS) is a collection of sensors, decision-making equipment and authorised protective measures used to detect and respond to potentially threatening unmanned aircraft.

Small aircraft can be difficult to notice, and not every airborne object is a drone. Consequently, counter-UAS operations require more than a single sensor. A radar may detect an object, while optical or infrared equipment helps determine what it is. Radio-frequency sensors can provide information about some transmitting devices.

At a conceptual level, protection involves detecting an object, checking its identity, tracking its movement, deciding whether action is authorised and assessing the result. The system must distinguish a genuine threat from birds, friendly aircraft and legitimate civilian activity.

Soft-kill and hard-kill measures

A soft-kill measure disrupts an unmanned aircraft's ability to perform its function without relying primarily on physical destruction. Interference with some communication or navigation functions is an example. A hard-kill measure physically disables or destroys the aircraft. These are broad categories of protective action, not different types of UAV.

Protective measures also introduce risks. Electronic interference can affect other legitimate users of the radio environment, while physical interception may create falling debris. Identification, lawful authority and the safety of nearby people are therefore essential considerations.

Indian example: DRDO's D4 system

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has developed the D4 counter-drone system. D4 is associated with the functions Drone Detect, Deter and Destroy. It combines different sensing functions with means of authorised counteraction. The Ministry of Defence described its detection, tracking and neutralisation capabilities in a release dated 24 January 2023.

Prelims focus

  • An autopilot is not proof of complete autonomy.
  • VLOS and BVLOS describe whether the aircraft remains within direct visual observation, not whether a pilot exists.
  • Navigation signals and the aircraft-control data link perform different functions.
  • Counter-UAS relies on detection, identification, tracking and authorised response.
  • Soft kill means functional disruption; hard kill means physical neutralisation.
  • DRDO's D4 is an Indian counter-drone system. Trap: A radar detection alone does not conclusively identify a drone.

[Sources: Ministry of Civil Aviation, Drone Rules, 2021, provisions concerning unmanned aircraft operation, notified 25 August 2021; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Anti-Drone System', 28 July 2021; 'Republic Day Parade 2023: DRDO to showcase tableau on surveillance, communication & neutralizing threats', 24 January 2023; DRDO, Technology Focus, July–August 2024, 'D4-Counter Drone System'; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Observations support detection and reliable identification, followed by tracking, an authority check, an authorised response and outcome assessment.
pictures.caption: Counter-UAS depends on reliable identification before any authorised protective response.

title: UAV Autonomy, Remote Piloting and Counter-Drone Systems

body:
What airworthiness means

Airworthiness is the condition in which an aircraft and its relevant systems meet the applicable safety and technical requirements for the intended operation.

Aircraft must be safe enough for their approved operating conditions. This involves more than whether an aircraft can briefly leave the ground. Its structure, controls, systems, documentation, maintenance and operating limitations must meet the relevant requirements.

Airworthiness also has a continuing aspect. An aircraft that was approved earlier can require inspection, maintenance or corrective action to remain fit for service. The fact that an aircraft once passed a test does not establish that it remains airworthy under all future conditions.

Initial and continuing airworthiness

Initial airworthiness

Initial airworthiness concerns demonstrating compliance with the technical requirements applicable to the aircraft's design and intended operation before it is approved for use.

Continuing airworthiness

Continuing airworthiness concerns keeping an approved aircraft in a condition that satisfies the relevant requirements throughout its service life. Appropriate maintenance, records, inspection and correction of identified problems are important to this process.

Important Indian organisations

India has different authorities and procedures for civil and military aviation. Their responsibilities should not be interchanged.

OrganisationFull namePrincipal association
CEMILACCentre for Military Airworthiness and CertificationMilitary airworthiness certification and technical evaluation
DGAQADirectorate General of Aeronautical Quality AssuranceQuality assurance, inspection and acceptance relating to military aeronautical products
DGCADirectorate General of Civil AviationCivil aviation regulation and applicable civil unmanned-aircraft certification

The Indian Military Airworthiness Procedure, 2023 (IMAP-2023), sets out the technical airworthiness framework for Indian military air systems. It defines responsibilities involving CEMILAC, DGAQA, manufacturers and the user services. The process covers different procurement and development situations; one organisation does not independently perform every aspect of certification, quality assurance and operational approval.

Development, testing, certification and induction

News about a new aircraft often refers to several milestones. They are not interchangeable:

  1. Development: The aircraft or system is being designed and made suitable for its intended purpose.
  2. Testing: Its behaviour, performance or compliance is being evaluated under specified conditions.
  3. Certification or technical clearance: The relevant authority determines that the applicable requirements have been met for a defined configuration or use.
  4. Delivery or acceptance: The customer formally receives or accepts the aircraft.
  5. Operational induction: The aircraft enters the service's operating organisation, subject to the service's arrangements and requirements.

These stages may overlap, and the exact process depends on the programme. A successful first flight is an important developmental milestone, but it is not automatically equivalent to certification or induction. Similarly, a signed procurement contract describes an order, not a completed delivery.

Military technical airworthiness and civil drone regulation have different institutional arrangements. The Drone Rules, 2021, do not apply to UAS belonging to, or used by, the naval, military or air forces of the Union of India. Do not assume that every military UAV follows the ordinary civil drone approval process, or that civil type certification is the same as operational permission for a military mission.

Prelims focus

  • CEMILAC stands for Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification.
  • DGAQA stands for Directorate General of Aeronautical Quality Assurance.
  • DGCA is the principal civil aviation regulator.
  • IMAP-2023 concerns Indian military airworthiness procedures.
  • Trap: First flight, certification, delivery and operational induction are not identical.

[Sources: DRDO, 'Indian Military Airworthiness Procedure (IMAP) 2023', Part 1, Ch. 1, 'Introduction to Indian Military Airworthiness', and Ch. 3, 'Military Air Systems/Airborne Stores Acquisition'; Ministry of Civil Aviation, Drone Rules, 2021; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Five aircraft milestones have distinct meanings; a successful first flight does not automatically establish certification or operational induction.
pictures.caption: A programme milestone must be identified before drawing conclusions about operational status.

title: Military Airworthiness and the Difference Between Testing and Induction

body:
Why navies operate different vessels

A navy must protect maritime interests, maintain surveillance, escort important shipping, provide rescue assistance and operate military forces at sea. No single type of vessel is equally suited to all these tasks. Naval platforms therefore differ in size, endurance, equipment and principal role.

Major categories of surface ships

Vessel typePrincipal roleImportant distinction
Aircraft carrierOperating military aircraft from the seaHas facilities for launching, recovering and supporting aircraft
DestroyerFleet protection and multiple combat rolesMajor surface combatant with substantial sensors and weapons
FrigateEscort and surface, air or submarine defenceMultipurpose warship commonly used for fleet and convoy protection
CorvettePatrol and combat duties, often in nearby seasGenerally smaller than major frigates and destroyers
Patrol vesselMaritime patrol, security and presenceUsually not equipped for the full range of major fleet combat duties
Amphibious vesselTransport and support of forces moving between sea and shoreDesigned around the movement of people, equipment or landing craft

Ship classifications are based on their design, equipment and intended role. There is no single worldwide tonnage rule that precisely separates every destroyer from every frigate. Modern vessels can perform overlapping missions, and a ship may carry helicopters without being an aircraft carrier.

Basic propulsion and ship systems

Many surface ships use diesel engines, gas turbines or combinations of propulsion systems. The engines ultimately drive propellers or other marine propulsors, either mechanically or through electrical arrangements.

A diesel engine converts energy from fuel combustion into mechanical power. A gas turbine also uses fuel combustion but produces power through a continuous flow of hot gases through the turbine. Ships may combine propulsion systems to meet different requirements for efficiency, speed and endurance.

A ship also depends on steering equipment, electrical power, navigation instruments, radar, communications and damage-control arrangements. A powerful propulsion system alone does not make a warship effective: it must be able to navigate, detect its surroundings, communicate and operate safely.

Aircraft carriers and flight-deck operations

An aircraft carrier is a warship equipped to operate aircraft at sea. It extends naval aviation beyond land-based airfields and supports tasks such as fleet air defence and maritime surveillance.

Aircraft carriers use different systems to launch and recover fixed-wing aircraft. Two important terms are:

  • STOBAR: Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery. Aircraft use a relatively short take-off run, commonly assisted by a ski-jump, and land using arresting equipment that slows them on the flight deck.
  • CATOBAR: Catapult Assisted Take-Off But Arrested Recovery. Aircraft receive launch assistance from a catapult and use arresting equipment for recovery.

These abbreviations describe aircraft launch-and-recovery arrangements, not submarine propulsion or ship radar systems. Helicopters, which can take off and land vertically, do not depend on the same fixed-wing take-off arrangement.

INS Vikrant: India's first indigenous aircraft carrier

INS Vikrant was commissioned on 2 September 2022 at Cochin Shipyard Limited, Kochi. It is India's first indigenous aircraft carrier and uses a STOBAR arrangement for suitable fixed-wing aircraft.

Calling Vikrant an indigenous aircraft carrier identifies its Indian shipbuilding programme. It does not mean that every individual component on the ship must be of Indian origin. It is also important not to confuse the newly built INS Vikrant with the earlier Indian aircraft carrier that bore the same name.

Indian warship examples commissioned together

On 15 January 2025, the Indian Navy commissioned 3 important platforms at Mumbai:

  • INS Surat: The 4th and final Project 15B guided-missile destroyer.
  • INS Nilgiri: The first Project 17A stealth frigate.
  • INS Vaghsheer: The 6th and final Project 75 Kalvari-class submarine.

Gujarat connection: INS Surat is named after the city of Surat in Gujarat. However, it was constructed at Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited in Mumbai, not at Surat. A ship's name does not necessarily identify its place of construction.

Prelims focus

  • INS Vikrant was commissioned on 2 September 2022 at Kochi and is India's first indigenous aircraft carrier.
  • INS Vikrant uses STOBAR, meaning Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery.
  • INS Surat is a Project 15B destroyer; INS Nilgiri is a Project 17A frigate.
  • INS Surat, INS Nilgiri and INS Vaghsheer were commissioned on 15 January 2025.
  • Trap: INS Surat was built in Mumbai, although it is named after a Gujarat city.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi commissions India's first indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant in Kochi', 2 September 2022; 'Indian Navy Set to Commission Three Frontline Fleet Assets Nilgiri, Surat and Vaghsheer', 1 January 2025; 'Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi dedicates to the nation frontline naval combatants INS Surat, INS Nilgiri & INS Vaghsheer in Mumbai', 15 January 2025; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A modern aircraft carrier sails with a naval jet and helicopter on its flight deck, accompanied by two distant escort warships.
pictures.caption: A carrier operates aircraft from the sea, while accompanying ships perform other naval roles.

pictures.alt: STOBAR uses a short run, commonly with a ski-jump; CATOBAR uses a catapult. Both use arrested recovery. INS Vikrant uses STOBAR.
